speaker: Siddhartha Mukherjee
title: The Alarming New Risks of Cancer Everyone Needs to Hear
question: In oncology drug discovery, how is AI actually used to generate viable new cancer medicines?
guest: You can't go into a general chatbot and say, 'Find me a medicine for breast cancer,' and out pops an answer. What you have to do is teach the AI the basic rules of medicinal chemistry, physics, and biology so it learns how to build a medicine the way humans do. Humans build medicines molecule by molecule: they identify and validate the cancer-relevant targets, and then they stitch together a molecule in three-dimensional space that can jam a lock and key on that target. Once the model speaks the language of medicinal chemistry, you can give it a potential target and it will generate not just one or two, but entire series of candidate medicines constrained by the laws of chemistry and physics. Then we have to test them in real life and feed that experimental data back to the AI—telling it where it was right and wrong—through reinforcement learning. We used to build medicines one at a time with human chemists; now we can make them many at a time.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: In oncology drug discovery, AI functions not as a standalone inventor, but as an engine driving the iterative design-make-test cycle. First, machine learning models analyze multi-omics, genomic, and clinical datasets to uncover novel tumor-specific targets and synthetic lethal vulnerabilities, while simultaneously identifying biomarkers to stratify the patients most likely to respond. Once a target is chosen, structural prediction models map 3D protein conformations and cryptic binding pockets, opening up historically "undruggable" cancer drivers. Generative AI architectures, such as diffusion models and transformers, then design *de novo* small molecules, therapeutic antibodies, or targeted protein degraders tailored directly to those pockets. Crucially, predictive algorithms evaluate millions of virtual structures in parallel to co-optimize potency alongside selectivity, solubility, metabolic stability, low off-target toxicity, and chemical synthesizability—ensuring healthy tissues are spared and molecules can actually be made. Rather than replacing wet-lab experimentation, these tools operate in closed-loop active learning cycles: top computational designs are synthesized and tested in automated cell and patient-derived organoid assays, with real-world biological results feeding back to refine the models until a viable clinical candidate emerges.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
AI mostly speeds up and improves specific steps in the usual drug discovery process. It doesn't invent finished cancer drugs on its own.

At the start, machine-learning models search genomic, CRISPR-screen, transcriptomic and patient data to find tumor dependencies and biomarkers worth targeting. Structure-prediction tools like AlphaFold, together with physics-based simulation, then model the target protein, including hidden pockets or mutant-specific shapes. Relay Therapeutics used protein-dynamics modeling to develop its mutant-selective PI3Kα inhibitor RLY-2608. Generative chemistry models then propose millions of candidate molecules. Predictive models score them for potency, selectivity, toxicity and pharmacokinetics, and the top few hundred are made and tested. Lab results go back into the models in repeated design-make-test cycles. This can shrink discovery from four to six years to about 12 to 30 months, with far fewer compounds synthesized. Examples include Schrödinger's MALT1 inhibitor SGR-1505, Iambic's HER2 drug IAM1363 and the CDK7 inhibitor REC-617, which Exscientia designed and Recursion now runs. AI also helps choose patients and design trials.

The key limit is that no AI-designed cancer drug has been approved as of my latest information. Phase 1 success rates look higher, but whether these drugs actually work is still decided in clinical trials.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: In oncology drug discovery, AI works as an iterative design-test-refine engine across the preclinical pipeline rather than a single black box. First, machine learning models integrate multi-omics tumor data, clinical records, and genetic perturbation screens to identify novel cancer-driving targets, synthetic-lethal vulnerabilities, and predictive patient biomarkers. Next, protein-folding and structure-prediction models map the three-dimensional shapes of those targets and reveal druggable binding pockets, even on historically difficult cancer proteins. Using those structures, generative models—such as diffusion architectures, graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning systems—either virtually screen massive chemical libraries or design novel small molecules, targeted protein degraders, and antibodies from scratch to fit the target precisely. Crucially, predictive models simultaneously optimize candidates for potency, selectivity, ease of synthesis, and drug-like absorption, metabolism, and toxicity profiles before anything is made. Chemists and biologists then synthesize and test the top candidates in cellular and animal assays, feeding experimental measurements back into the models to refine subsequent generations until a viable clinical candidate emerges.

noweb.answer: In oncology drug discovery, AI accelerates and guides multiple stages of turning biological hypotheses into clinical candidates rather than designing drugs in isolation. First, machine learning models analyze multi-omic tumor data, genomics, and biomedical literature to identify novel cancer-driving targets and synthetic-lethal vulnerabilities. Once a target is chosen, structural prediction tools like AlphaFold help model protein conformations and reveal druggable binding pockets, even for historically difficult targets. Generative AI models—such as diffusion, transformer, and reinforcement-learning systems—then design novel small molecules, biologics, or antibody sequences tailored to fit those pockets while optimizing potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties. In parallel, predictive models filter out candidates likely to fail due to poor absorption, off-target toxicity, or metabolic instability, and suggest efficient synthetic routes for chemists. Crucially, AI operates in an iterative "design-make-test-analyze" loop: computational candidates are synthesized and tested in wet-lab assays, and those experimental results continually retrain the models until a viable preclinical medicine emerges.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
AI helps oncology teams decide which drug candidates to make and test. It can analyze tumor genetics and experimental data to identify proteins that cancer cells depend on, then screen existing compounds or propose new molecules designed to act on those proteins. Models rank candidates by predicted potency, selectivity, solubility, and how the body might absorb and metabolize them.

Researchers synthesize the most promising candidates and test them in biochemical assays, cancer cells, and sometimes patient-derived organoids. They feed the results back into the models to guide the next round of design. A molecule that kills cancer cells but also harms healthy cells, for example, can be redesigned or dropped. Candidates that survive this cycle still need preclinical safety studies and clinical trials to establish whether they can safely benefit patients. AI makes the search more focused. Experiments and trials determine which candidates become medicines.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
AI helps researchers decide which molecules to make and test. It can analyze genetic data from tumors and results from lab experiments to identify a protein that cancer cells depend on. Once researchers select a target, AI can screen existing compounds or propose new chemical structures. Models help prioritize molecules predicted to bind the target, spare similar proteins, and reach the tumor at an effective concentration.

Chemists then make the most promising candidates and test them. A molecule might bind its target tightly but break down too quickly in the body. Researchers can feed those measurements back into the model to suggest changes, then make and test the revised molecules. This cycle can reduce the number of compounds a team needs to synthesize. Preclinical studies assess whether a candidate is ready for human testing, and clinical trials determine whether it benefits patients at an acceptable level of risk.
